families.s: HSE refuse-collection route and pedestrian transport-safety guidance
families.t: route planning, pedestrians, narrow streets, high-footfall locations, reversing, crew positioning, visibility, public protection and vehicle operation
f: Refuse collection vehicles are involved in serious and often fatal pedestrian incidents.
Pedestrian safety should be a primary objective when collection routes are planned and managed.
Narrow streets, pedestrianised areas and locations near schools or transport hubs require advance consideration.
Vehicle routes and collection methods should reduce reversing wherever practicable.
Crew members should have defined safe positions and communication arrangements during vehicle movement.
Visibility limitations and blind spots should be assessed for the vehicle and route.
The collection system should protect workers, residents, visitors and other road users.
Route risk assessments should be reviewed when vehicles, bins, timing, traffic or street conditions change.
families.g: Collection-route risk depends on route and traffic, pedestrian density, vehicle design and visibility, reversing and crew position, collection method, time, weather, communication and supervision.

families.s: HSE waste-collection manual-handling, sharps and hygiene guidance
families.t: manual handling, slips, falling objects, moving machinery, sharps, contamination, handwashing, vehicle hygiene facilities and PPE
f: Collection work has significant risks from manual handling, slips, falls and moving or falling objects.
Needlestick and other sharp-object injuries are a recognised collection hazard.
Waste health hazards can enter by skin contact, sharps injection, ingestion or inhalation.
Collection-system design should minimise unnecessary lifting, carrying, pulling and repetitive handling.
Suitable high-visibility and cut-resistant protection may be required for residual risks.
Vehicle hygiene facilities should be selected through a COSHH-based risk assessment.
The assessment should reflect waste type, contamination level, containment, exposure route and collection location.
Workers should open sacks or containers only as needed and remain away from tipping points where airborne contamination is released.
families.g: Collection-health risk depends on waste and containment, load and handling frequency, sharp and biological contamination, tipping and dust, route conditions, hygiene facilities, PPE and training.

families.s: HSE prevention of people being tipped from large bins into collection vehicles
families.t: bin access, vulnerable occupants, secure storage, access restrictors, pre-empty checks, compactor stop, warning signs, behaviour and emergency response
f: People sheltering or sleeping in large commercial bins have been killed or nearly killed during emptying.
Controls should reduce the likelihood of people gaining access to bins.
Bins should be checked for occupants before they are lifted or emptied.
Collection workers must know how to stop the compactor immediately if a person is tipped into the vehicle.
Waste producers should locate bins in secure areas where practicable.
Where access is foreseeable, suitable lid locks, restrictors, grilles or other access controls should be considered.
Warning signs can support the system but are not a substitute for physical and procedural controls.
Emergency procedures should consider frightened, disorientated or aggressive behaviour by a rescued occupant.
families.g: Large-bin occupant risk depends on bin type and location, access and evidence of occupation, physical restrictors, inspection and communication, compactor controls, worker training and emergency response.

families.s: HSE waste-vehicle hoists, skip loaders and hookloader lifting-operation guidance
families.t: LOLER, hoists, hooks, cylinders, pipework, skip lugs, examination, blind spots, exclusion zones, jogging and defect checks
f: Hoists on refuse vehicles and lifting equipment on skip loaders and hookloaders are lifting equipment under LOLER.
These mechanisms generally require periodic thorough examination by a competent person.
Skip lugs, bottle-bank wires and other load attachment points are safety-critical and require maintenance.
The lifting hook, hydraulic cylinders, pipework and fittings should be treated as safety-critical components.
People should be kept clear of the vehicle, container and load throughout loading, unloading and reversing.
Large skips and containers create rear blind spots that may require cameras, radar or other controls.
Jogging a vehicle with a raised skip can cause uncontrolled movement or component failure and should not be used as an improvised release method.
Pre-use defect checks and planned maintenance should identify leakage, creep, damage and deterioration.
families.g: Waste lifting risk depends on vehicle and hoist type, load and container condition, lifting points and hydraulics, examination and maintenance, visibility, exclusion, operating method and competence.

families.s: HSE waste-transfer-station transport segregation and vehicle-assisted hand-sorting guidance
families.t: fixed-site layout, pedestrians, mobile plant, totting, floor picking, shovels, segregation, visibility, supervision and public access
f: Waste-transfer stations have a high risk of serious workplace-transport incidents.
Fixed-site layout and management systems can substantially reduce vehicle-movement risk.
Pedestrians should be adequately segregated from vehicles and mobile plant.
Vehicle-assisted floor picking or totting exposes hand sorters to mechanical shovels and other mobile plant.
Several fatal incidents have occurred where effective segregation was not achieved.
Hand sorting should be eliminated from active vehicle areas where reasonably practicable.
Where interaction remains, controlled zones, communication, visibility aids and supervision are required.
Site rules should cover visiting drivers, public users, reversing, loading, tipping and abnormal operations.
families.g: Transfer-station risk depends on layout and traffic flow, mobile plant and visibility, pedestrian and public presence, sorting method, segregation, communication, supervision and changing stockpiles.
